unplaced.text: Τόπον κατάσκιον. Tritissimæ voces κατάσκιος et κατασκιάζειν. Quarum ultimam reduci velim in locum suum, apud Palladium, Dialogo de vita S. Chrysostomi, cap. 18, p. 178 : Εἰς ὕπνον κατέπεσεν, οὔτε τοίχου ἢ πέτρας σκιὰν εὑρίσκων, ἀλλ᾽ ὑπὸ φυτὸν ἀρκεύθινον, ὃ καὶ αὐτὸ ἀμυδρῶς κατασκιάζει. Minime vero κατασκευάζει. Elias in somnum decidit, neque parietis aut saxi inveniens umbram, sed sub juniperi virgulto, quod et ipsum exiliter obumbrat. Nec minus in voce haud absimili erratum t. II Auct. Combef. c. 237 D. In Andreæ Cretensis lambis, φωτὸς καταστράπτοντος αὐτοὺς ἀσκίου. Quos fulguris, lux, in modum blande subit. Cum edendum fuisset ἀσκίου. Φῶς ἄσκιον lumen significat divinum quod umbra caret. Lumine umbræ experte collustrante ipsos.
unplaced.anchorLine: κατάσκιον (d), προσδοχῶντες τὸν ἐκ τῆς δίψης θάνα-
unplaced.en: 'A shady place.' The words κατάσκιος and κατασκιάζειν are very common. I should like the latter restored to its place in Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom, ch. 18, p. 178: 'He fell asleep, finding no shade of wall or rock, but under a juniper bush, which itself shades only faintly.' Certainly not κατασκευάζει. Elias fell asleep, finding no shade of wall or rock, but under a juniper shrub, which itself shades but thinly. There is no less an error in a similar word in Combefis, Auctarium, vol. 2, col. 237 D: in the iambs of Andrew of Crete, 'φωτὸς καταστράπτοντος αὐτοὺς ἀσκίου' (of a shadowless light flashing upon them): 'whom the light of lightning gently comes upon', when ἀσκίου should have been printed. 'Φῶς ἄσκιον' signifies the divine light that lacks shadow: 'with a light free of shadow shining upon them.'

unplaced.text: Καυκίῳ. Καυκίον et καυκάλιον infra, cap. 15, ut καῦκος et καῦκα, idem sonant ac Latine caucus, caucum, cauculus, caucellus ; id est calix, scyphus, poculum, patera et vas cavum. Circa quæ omissis aliorum animadversionibus, unum expendam locum, ex Indice ad Nicetæ Annales petitum, Καύκαλον, μίμημα, p. 95 C, ubi narratur de Aarone mago et dicitur : Καὶ προῦχειτο χελώνης ἐκφορον μίμημα, ἔνδον στέγον τῆς χέλυος ἀνθρωπόμορφον εἴκασμα, πεπεδημένον ἄμφω τὼ πόδε, καὶ τὸ στέρνον ἐληλαμένον ἥλῳ διαμπερές. Interpr. : Et simulacrum testudinis prolatum, in quo erat imago hominis, qui ambos pedes habebat in compedibus et pectus clavo transfixum. Verum καύκαλον, vel ut forte scribendum est καυκάλινον, et μίμημα nullatenus quadrant, sed μίμημα respondet voci sequenti εἴκασμα nisi si pro καύκαλον vitiose legerit εἴκελον. Nicetas itaque, mea quidem sententia, explicari debet de cauco et vase concavo ; illiusque verba hoc pacto in Latinum sermonem sunt transferenda : Et depromptum prostabat testudineum vasculum, intra testudinem tegens humanæ formæ imaginem, utroque pede compeditam, et per totum pectus clavo confixam. Nec me præteriit, Salmasium hominem longe doctissimum aliter sentire in Notis ad Spartianum, atque χελώνης καύκαλον exponere testudinis superficiem, quod mihi ideo non placet, tum quia non solum proferebatur superficies testudinis, sed testudo ipsa seu vas e testudine, tum quia coactius videtur interpretamentum. Cogitet etiam prudens lector, utrum in eodem Nicetæ Indice καῦκα, quæ καῦκα est ac ἑταιρίς, erratum sit descriptoris : non enim ausim affirmare, ut et dubito de his in Vita Eudociæ martyris n. 2, Martii 1 : Γέγονε καυκίον ἀμόλυντος, quia vestigia ms. lectionis magis premeret καὶ ὀχεῖον.
unplaced.anchorLine: τὸ χεῖλος τῆς κολυμβήθρας, καὶ ἐν ξυλίνῳ καυκίῳ (e)
unplaced.en: 'In a cup.' Καυκίον and καυκάλιον below, ch. 15, like καῦκος and καῦκα, sound the same as Latin caucus, caucum, cauculus, caucellus, that is, a cup, goblet, drinking vessel, dish and hollow vessel. Passing over others' remarks on these, I shall weigh one passage, taken from the Index to the Annals of Nicetas, under Καύκαλον, 'likeness', p. 95 C, where Aaron the magician is described: 'And there was set forth a likeness of a tortoise, within the tortoise-shell a man-shaped image, with both feet fettered and the breast driven through with a nail.' Latin version: 'And a likeness of a tortoise was brought forth, in which was the image of a man who had both feet in fetters and his breast pierced by a nail.' But καύκαλον (or perhaps one should write καυκάλινον) and μίμημα do not fit at all; rather μίμημα corresponds to the following word εἴκασμα, unless the writer misread εἴκελον for καύκαλον. Nicetas therefore, in my opinion, should be explained of a cup and a hollow vessel, and his words rendered into Latin thus: 'And a little tortoise-shell vessel was brought out, covering inside the shell an image of human form, bound by both feet and pierced through the whole breast by a nail.' I am aware that Salmasius, a very learned man, thinks otherwise in his Notes on Spartianus and explains χελώνης καύκαλον as the surface of the tortoise-shell; I dislike this both because not only the surface of the shell was brought forth but the tortoise itself or a vessel of shell, and because the interpretation seems forced. Let the prudent reader also consider whether in the same Index of Nicetas καῦκα, which is the same as ἑταιρίς, is a copyist's error; I dare not affirm it, and I likewise doubt the passage in the Life of Eudocia the martyr, n. 2, March 1: 'Γέγονε καυκίον ἀμόλυντος', since the traces of the manuscript reading would lean more toward 'καὶ ὀχεῖον'.

Severus is Latin, which in Greek is heretic', and to annotate that he did not know whether Severus is the same as Heretic. Goar, however, interpreted it of something harsh, rigid, deadly, which could therefore be called αἱρετικός or perhaps ἀναιρετικός.

Sagittarius vir equinis cruribus deformatur, cui sagittam et arcum adjungunt, ut ex eo mensis ipsius fulmina demonstrentur. Unde et sagittarius est vocatus. Quæ ideo protuli, ut per ea tollerem mendum forte typographicum e Rabano libro De computo, cap. 59. t. I Miscellaneorum Baluzianorum : Scorpium et Sagittarium equinis cruribus deformatum, propter flumina (fulmina) mensium ipsorum, October et November accipiunt. Huc etiam pertinere potest locus turpissimo mendo deformatus, epist. 38 Theophylacti, ἵνα ταύτῃ καὶ τῷ διεγγίζοις, καὶ τοῦ κεραυνοῦ τηροῖο ἀπείρατος ex interprete : Ut hoc pacto ad illud saltem propius accedas, et ab ingenti fulmine, te illius penitus inexpertem tuteris. Atque ita emaculandus τῷ Διὶ ἐγγίζοις. Ex vulgari adagio, πόρρω Διός τε καὶ κεραυνοῦ. De quo Parœmiographi, et Synesius, De regno, p. 11, ex cujus textu Suidas et Michael Apostolus corrigi debent.
unplaced.anchorLine: Καὶ μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας, ἀστραπῆς (z) γενομένης με-
unplaced.en: Astrapes (lightning). Isidore, Origines III, last chapter: they called Scorpio and Sagittarius after the lightnings of that month; Sagittarius is a man with horse's legs, given a bow and arrow so that the month's lightnings may be indicated. The editor cites these to remove a probable printer's error in Rabanus, De computo ch. 59 (Baluze, Miscellanea I): 'flumina' should be 'fulmina'. The same may apply to a badly corrupt passage in Theophylact, epist. 38: it should be emended to 'τῷ Διὶ ἐγγίζοις' ('you would approach Zeus'), from the common saying 'far from Zeus and the thunderbolt', treated by the paroemiographers and by Synesius, De regno, p. 11, from whose text Suidas and Michael Apostolus ought to be corrected.

Phavorinus, βυρσάτονος, τοῦ τυμπάνου. Castigandum opinor, βύρσα, τόνος τυμπάνου.

unplaced.en: Brontes (thunder). It is better to consult the ancients than to trust even very learned moderns. So from Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I, and Tzetzes, Chiliad 7, v. 91, Salmoneus's thunders will be 'from a hide' (ἐκ βύρσης), not 'ἐκ κύρσης', as in the Life of Nicephorus of CP by Ignatius the deacon, n. 81, at 13 March; Hesychius has 'byrsatonos, a drum'; or in another edition 'byrsas, tonos, drum'; Phavorinus 'byrsatonos, of the drum'. unplaced.text: Τὰ φολερά. Et cap. iii, hic, φόλεις, φολερά. Usitatum φόλεις. Rarum φολερά. Unde fuit depravatum, cap. 83 Joannis nostri, ἀπὸ φαλερῶν ε'. Quod non intelligens Ambrosius Camaldulensis interpres, nec valens emendare, penitus omisit. In Chronico Marcellini, Nummis, quos Romani Terentianos vel Teruncianos vocant, Græci follares, aut follerales. Anastasius princeps suo nomine figuralis, placibilem plebi commutationem distraxit.
unplaced.anchorLine: τὰ φολερά (f)
unplaced.en: Ta folera. Also ch. 3 here: folleis, folera. Folleis is the usual form, folera the rare one. Hence it was corrupted in ch. 83 of our John to 'apo phaleron 5'. Ambrose of Camaldoli, the translator, not understanding it and unable to emend it, omitted it entirely. In the Chronicle of Marcellinus: coins which the Romans call Terentiani or Teruncianii, the Greeks follares or follerales. The emperor Anastasius, under his own name, devised a figured coin changing it to one pleasing to the people.

unplaced.text: Σιωπήσας τὸ σύνολον. A Meursio editus Eusebius, in Canticum canticorum, p. 42 : Ἀποδεκτικὴ δέ ἐστιν σιωπὴ, ἐν τῷ ἐπιστημόνως κρύπτοντι, καὶ τῷ μισουμένῳ τὰ θειότερα, καὶ μείζω τῆς τῶν ἀκροατῶν δυνάμεως. Non dubito quin scribendum sit, ἀποδεκτή, et μυουμένῳ vel μυομένῳ et ἀκροατῶν. Id est : Laudandum porro est silentium, in eo qui perite celat, quique diviniora et auditorum vires superantia edoctus est, aut occultat.
unplaced.anchorLine: δύο ἡμέρας νηστεύων, καὶ σιωπήσας (g) τὸ σύνολον, μήτε λαλήσας πρός τινα.
unplaced.en: Having kept silence altogether. Eusebius, On the Song of Songs, edited by Meursius, p. 42: "Silence is acceptable in one who conceals knowledgeably, and to one who hates the diviner things, and what is greater than the power of the hearers." I do not doubt that one should write apodekte (acceptable), and myoumeno or myomeno (initiated), and akroaton (hearers). That is: silence is to be praised in one who conceals skilfully, who has been taught things too divine and beyond the hearers' strength, or hides them.

unplaced.text: Διέκρινε τὸ κοινωνῆσαι et κοινωνῆσαι διακρίνομαι. Hinc Diacrinomeni, hæretici, quorum mentio apud Leontium, De sectis, act. 4, 5, 6 et 7 ; Photium, cod. 24 ; Nicephorum, Hist. lib. xviii, cap. 45. Præcipue vero memoratur Joannes Diacrinomenus, cujus Historia ecclesiastica citatur act. 5 concilii generalis septimi. Ἰωάννης, inquit Theodorus Lector, lib. ii ὁ Διακρινόμενος μετὰ Σεβήρου ἱστορεῖ. Seu potius meo quidem judicio κατὰ Σεβήρου, adversus Severum, quamvis Nicephorus legisse se μετὰ ostendat, dum scribit, lib. xvi, cap. 29. Ἱστορεῖ δὲ Ἰωάννης ὁ αὐτῷ (Σεβήρῳ) διακρινόμενος. Quinetiam hujus Historiæ meminit Photius, Bibliothecæ cap. 41 ; sed quod conjicit esse Joannis presbyteri Ægeatæ, graviter errat : siquidem Joannes Ægeates vel Ægeota Nestorianus fuit, auctore ipso Photio, cod. 55 et Leontio act. 9 ; utque legitur in libello Precum ante epistolam Hormisdæ, 75 ; et in concilio generali 6, act. 11 et 15. Historicus autem Joannes Diacrinomenus, oppositæ prorsus hæreseos, necnon juxta Photium laudator conciliabuli Ephesini, Dioscori et sociorum. Denique in Demonstrationibus chronicis, quas exhibuit publico usui Franc. Combefisius, ὁ Διακρινόμενος est Joannes iste.
unplaced.anchorLine: Ἱεροσολύμων, καὶ διέκρινε τὸ κοινωνῆσαι αὐτῷ (r). Ἐν
unplaced.en: On Διέκρινε τὸ κοινωνῆσαι: κοινωνῆσαι and διακρίνομαι. Hence the Diacrinomeni, heretics, mentioned in Leontius, De sectis, acts 4, 5, 6 and 7; Photius, cod. 24; Nicephorus, Hist. bk 18, ch. 45. Chiefly remembered is John Diacrinomenus, whose Ecclesiastical History is cited in act 5 of the seventh general council. 'John,' says Theodore Lector, bk 2, 'the Diacrinomenus, writes with Severus' (μετὰ Σεβήρου). Or rather, in my judgment, κατὰ Σεβήρου, against Severus, although Nicephorus shows that he read μετά, when he writes, bk 16, ch. 29: 'John, who was at odds with him (Severus), writes.' Photius, Bibliotheca ch. 41, also mentions this History; but his conjecture that it is by John the priest of Aegae is a grave mistake, since John of Aegae (or Aegeota) was a Nestorian, on the authority of Photius himself, cod. 55, and of Leontius act 9, and as is read in the Libellus of Prayers before the letter of Hormisdas, 75, and in general council 6, acts 11 and 15. The historian John Diacrinomenus, by contrast, was of the directly opposite heresy and, according to Photius, a praiser of the conciliabulum of Ephesus, of Dioscorus and his partisans. Finally, in the Chronicle Demonstrations which Francis Combefis made public, ὁ Διακρινόμενος is this John.

unplaced.en: On Κρούσαι τὸ ξύλον ('to strike the wooden board'): in Allatius, De confessione utriusque Ecclesiae, col. 1560: 'he strikes the striking'; col. 1569: 'to make a striking.' In the Life of St Sabas: 'the hour of the striking.' And in the iambics of Theodore of Studium: 'when the board is being struck.' And: 'Sound the board in season.' And: 'whenever someone sounds the board.' By metaphor, as in Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite: 'those who have not been summoned by the trumpet of the sacred rites,' i.e. when the trumpet has sounded for the assembly. In the Rule of St Pachomius, n. 2; Anastasius at act 4 of the Seventh Council: 'Easterners strike wood in place of bells.'

unplaced.text: Ἀβάλλαι. Cap. 49 et 78, ἀβάλε. Sic enim quoque solet efferri, atque etiam ἀββάλε. Estque notissima ex grammaticis dictio. Pseudo-Theophilus Alexandrinus, seu pseudo-Chrysostomus Savilii, t. VIII, c. 857, qui ex multis variarum bibliothecarum codicibus verus est · Christophorus Alexandrinus, sermone, Cui vita humana sit similis : Ἀβάλε τῇ ἀνθρωπότητι, ἀβάλε μοι ; Gregentius, f. 25 : Ἀβάλε ὅτι τὰς ἀσθενείας ὑμῶν ἐβάστασε · Theodorus Studita Laudatione in tertiam inventionem capitis sancti Joannis Baptistæ : Ἀβάλαι τοῦ ἀσελγεστάτου συμποσίου ! Proh impudicissimum convivium ! In sanctum Platonem, n. 27 : Vah ! ob ea quæ gesta tunc fuerunt. Apage facinora tunc temporis perpetrata ! Constantinus, De administratione imperii, paulo ante finem, p. 228 : Ἀβάλα λοιπὸν τῷ πιστεύοντι Χερσωνίτῃ πολίτῃ. Ubi Meursio est vox non intellecta. Sed aut legendum ἀβάλαι, aut ἀβάλαι per apocopen transiit in ἀβάλα, ut et in ἄβαλ apud Phavorinum et in Etymologico mayno. Epigrammate 70 Paradisi Joannis Geometræ, Ἀββάλε Μεζώης ! Atque eodem modo malim accipere in Metaphrasi Apollinaris, psal. lxviii, 8 : Ἀββάλε, πῶς τὸ πάροιθεν ἄναξ ἡγήσατο λαῶν ! quam cum interprete pro ἀνάβαλε, cunctare. Vid. Damascenum, De fidelibus defunctis, in fine.
unplaced.anchorLine: Εἶπεν πάλιν· Ἀβάλαι (u), πόσα κλαύσομεν, καὶ
unplaced.en: On Ἀβάλαι: in chapters 49 and 78, ἀβάλε. So too it is commonly pronounced, and also ἀββάλε. A very well-known word from the grammarians. Pseudo-Theophilus of Alexandria, or pseudo-Chrysostom in Savile, vol. 8, col. 857, who is true from many codices of various libraries; Christophorus of Alexandria, in the sermon 'To what is human life like?': 'Ἀβάλε to humanity, ἀβάλε to me'; Gregentius, fol. 25: 'Ἀβάλε, for he bore your weaknesses'; Theodore of Studium, in the Praise on the Third Finding of the Head of St John the Baptist: 'Ἀβάλαι of the most licentious banquet! Oh, shameless feast!' In 'On St Plato', n. 27: 'Ah! for the things done then. Away with the crimes then committed!' Constantine, De administratione imperii, a little before the end, p. 228: 'Ἀβάλα, then, to the believing Cherson citizen.' Where Meursius says it is a word not understood. But either ἀβάλαι must be read, or ἀβάλαι passed by apocope into ἀβάλα, as also into ἄβαλ in Phavorinus and in the Etymologicum Magnum. In epigram 70 of the Paradisus of John Geometres: 'Ἀββάλε Μεζώης!' I would prefer to take it likewise in the Metaphrasis of Apollinaris, Psalm 68 (LXVIII), 8: 'Ἀββάλε, how the leader formerly led the peoples!' which the interpreter renders as ἀνάβαλε, 'delay.' See Damascenus, On the faithful departed, at the end.

unplaced.text: Ἔνιψεν αὐτοῦ τοὺς πόδας. Quod spectat ad loturam pedum, afferam insignem ad Origenem emendationem, tom. 32, in Joannem p. 347-375: Καὶ ὁ εὐαγγελιστὴς γε ἐν τούτοις μοι δοκεῖ διεγείρων ἡμῶν τὸν νοῦν ἐπὶ τῶν νοερῶν τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον, μὴ τετηρηκέναι μὲν σωματικὴν περὶ τοῦ νίψασθαι τὴν ἀκολουθίαν. Ita edidit præstantissimus et celeberrimus vir Petrus Daniel Huetius, conjectura facta ex hisce codicis Reg. Ἐν τοὺς μοι δοκεῖ. Mihi vero perplacet, ἔνθους μοι. Et verto: Quin et evangelista numine afflatus, videtur mihi, excitans mentem nostram ad intelligentiam spiritualem præsentis loci, non observasse corporalem lavandi consequentiam. Vita Joannis Chrysostomi, ab incerto seu anonymo scripta, p. 324, l. xxi, loco insigni, obscuro, per doctissimum clarissimumque Savilium non intellecto, et eapropter apponendo hic: Τούτοις ὁ μέγας καταπλαγεὶς, καὶ ἔνθους ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῖς εἰρημένοις γενόμενος, ἀνεσκόπει· καὶ γάρ πως ἡ ψυχὴ τὸ χρηματιζόμενον. Id est, His magnus ille perculsus, et velut ad ea verba divinitus inspiratus, considerabat. Ipsius etenim anima quodammodo admonebatur. Sed ut ad rem redeam, quid sit balatoforum in testamento sancti Remigii, apud Flodoardum, lib. i, cap. 28, nemo, quod sciam, docuit: Aliis pauperibus tribus, ubi fratres quotidie pedes lavare debent, quibus etiam balatoforum, quod dicitur, xenodochium, ad hoc ministerium statui, solidus unus dabitur. Nec ego possum explicare monstrum lectionis; duntaxat possum per conjecturam corrigere, scribendo balnaforum aut balaneophorum, βαλανειοφόρον, quod ita a balneo et lavacro dictum sit.
unplaced.anchorLine: ἐνέγκας ὕδωρ, ἔνιψεν αὐτοῦ τοὺς πόδας (a), καὶ δι'
unplaced.en: On 'He washed his feet.' As regards the washing of feet, I shall bring forward a notable emendation of Origen, vol. 32, On John, pp. 347-375: [Greek: the evangelist, it seems to me, in these things, rousing our mind to the spiritual realities of the place, did not observe the bodily sequence concerning the washing]. So the most distinguished and celebrated Pierre-Daniel Huet edited it, by a conjecture made from these words of the Royal codex, 'Ἐν τοὺς μοι δοκεῖ.' To me 'ἔνθους μοι' is preferable. And I translate: 'Indeed the evangelist too, inspired by the divine breath, seems to me to be rousing our mind to the spiritual understanding of the present passage, and not to have observed the bodily order of the washing.' In the Life of John Chrysostom, written by an unknown or anonymous author, p. 324, l. 21, a notable passage which the most learned and illustrious Savile did not understand and which is therefore added here: [Greek: Struck by these things, and as though inspired by what had been said, he reflected; for his soul in some way ...the oracle]. That is: 'Greatly struck by these things, and as if divinely inspired by those words, he pondered. For his soul was in a way being admonished.' But to return to the matter, nobody to my knowledge has explained what 'balatoforum' is in the testament of St Remigius, in Flodoard, bk. 1, ch. 28: 'To three other poor persons, where the brothers daily must wash feet, to whom also of the balatoforum, as it is called, of the xenodochium, I have appointed for this service one solidus.' I cannot explain the monstrous reading, but I can only correct it by conjecture, writing 'balnaforum' or 'balaneophorum' (βαλανειοφόρον), so called from bath and washing-place.

unplaced.text: Βλάπτειν. Non sine indignatione leges ista apud Cyrillum ad Joan. xii, 46, p. 691: Καὶ ἵνα αὐτοὶ μὴ ἰσχύοντες βλέψαι τὸν οὐδὲν ἀδικήσαντα, τοὺς δυνατωτέρους κατ' αὐτοῦ ἐρεθίσωσι· Utque cum ipsi non possent in os intueri eum qui nihil injustum fecerat, potentiores adversus eum irritarent atque accenderent. Quanta enim ἀβλεψία, non percepisse βλάψαι, lædere eum qui nulla injuria affecerat.
unplaced.anchorLine: ἢ τίς ἰσχύει βλάπτειν (b);
unplaced.en: 'To harm.' You will not read this without indignation in Cyril on John 12:46, p. 691: [Greek: And so that they themselves, being unable to look upon the man who had done no wrong, might stir up the more powerful against him]; that is, since they could not look in the face the one who had done nothing unjust, they would provoke and inflame the more powerful against him. How great the blindness, not to have grasped what it is to harm one who has done no injury.

unplaced.text: Τῶν ἔμπροσθεν. Philipp. iii, 14: Ἓν δέ, τὰ μὲν ὀπίσω ἐπιλανθανόμενος, τοῖς δὲ ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτεινόμενος, κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκω ἐπὶ τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. Unum autem, quæ quidem retro sunt obliviscens, ad ea vero quæ sunt priora extendens meipsum, ad destinatum persequor, ad bravium supernæ vocationis Dei in Christo Jesu. Ad quæ respiciens Cæsarius, quæst. 171, scripserat: Ὁ γὰρ πολὺς ἐκεῖνος καὶ ὑψηλὸς τὴν διάνοιαν, ἀεὶ διὰ ταύτης θέων οὐδέποτε τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτεινόμενος ἔληξεν. Hoc est, Magnus enim ille et mente excelsus, per hanc (virtutem) perpetuo currens, nunquam ad ea quæ priora sunt extendere se cessavit. At bellis hominibus placuit edere ἐπεκτεινομένοις ἔλεξεν, cum hac versione sua, nunquam ad ulteriora se pervenisse dixit. I nunc, et linguæ Græcæ notitiam neglige, ut editionibus fideas, auctores Græcos intelligas.
unplaced.anchorLine: βλέποντες εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω, τῶν ἔμπροσθεν (b') ἐπιλαν-
unplaced.en: 'Of the things before.' Philippians 3:14: [quoted in Greek and Latin: one thing, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus]. Caesarius, question 171, had written with this in view: [Greek: for that great man, lofty in mind, running always through this virtue, never ceased stretching forward to what lies ahead]. That is: that great man, exalted in mind, running continually by this (virtue), never ceased to stretch himself toward the things that were before. But certain fine people saw fit to print 'ἐπεκτεινομένοις ἔλεξεν', and with this translation of theirs said that he never reached anything further. Go on then, and neglect knowledge of Greek, so that you may trust the editions and understand the Greek authors!

unplaced.text:
Βαΐν, seu βαΐον. Remittam te ad alios, ubi posuero scholium seu observatiunculam cod. Reg. 1067, f. 212.
Βαΐα διὰ τί λέγονται οἱ κλάδοι τῶν φοινίκων; Ἐπειδὴ τῇ Ἑβραίων φωνῇ ἡ σελήνη βαΐον ὀνομάζεται. Ὁ γοῦν φοῖνιξ τὸ δένδρον καθ' ἑκάστην πρόοδον τῆς σελήνης, ἣν τινες γένναν καλοῦσιν, ἐκ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ καρδίας ἀναδίδωσι· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τούτους τοὺς κλάδους τῶν φοινίκων, Ἑβραῖοι, βαΐα προσαγορεύουσιν· ἀπὸ τοῦ περὶ τὸ δένδρον συμβαίνοντος παραδόξου κατωνομάζοντες. Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐξ ἐκείνων παραλαβόντες, καλοῦμεν αὐτὰ βαΐα.
Quamobrem rami palmarum, βαΐα dicuntur? Quia Hebræorum lingua luna nominatur βαΐον. Itaque palma arbor, quolibet lunæ processu, quem nonnulli nativitatem vocant, ex suo corde ramos producit: eaque de causa ramos illos palmarum, Hebræi βαΐα nuncupant; ab inopino quod arbori contingit denominantes. Simili ratione et nos ab illis accipientes βαΐα indigitamus.
Aliter Callistus in Synaxario: Ἐδήλουν δὲ διὰ τῶν βαΐων, οἱονεὶ τῶν κλάδων. Βαΐον γὰρ παρ' Ἑβραίοις ὁ ἁπλοῦς κλάδος λέγεται. In Triodio Græcorum, τῶν βαΐων Sabbato, βαΐον παρ' Ἑβραίοις ὁ ἁπαλὸς κλάδος λέγεται. Grammatici Græci deducunt, παρὰ τὸ βίᾳ τίλλεσθαι. Balsamoni vox latina est, aliis Ægyptia. Sed quis nescit nugas etymologistarum? Chronici Alexandrini vocati, p. 7821: Καὶ προσῆλθεν τῷ βασιλεῖ Οὐαλεντινιανῷ ἡ γυνὴ τῷ βαΐῳ πρωΐ. Lege vel σὺν τῷ βαΐῳ, vel βαΐων. Et accessit mulier cum palma mane ad imperatorem Valentinianum. Aut: Et accessit ad imperatorem Valentinianum mulier mane festi Palmarum.
unplaced.anchorLine: τοῦ τὸ βαΐν (f), ἀνέστησαν οἱ τοῦ μέρους αὐτοῦ κρά-
unplaced.en: 'Baïn' or 'baïon.' I shall refer you to others, where I have set down a scholium or little observation from Royal codex 1067, f. 212. [Scholium:] Why are the branches of palm trees called baia? Because in the Hebrew tongue the moon is called baion. The palm tree, at each advance of the moon (which some call the 'birth'), puts forth branches from its own heart; and for that reason the Hebrews call these palm branches baia, naming them from the marvel that happens to the tree. Likewise we, having received them from those people, call them baia. [Latin version of the same.] Otherwise, Callistus in the Synaxarion: 'They signified by the baia, as it were, the branches. For among the Hebrews the simple branch is called baion.' In the Triodion of the Greeks, on the Sabbath of the palms: 'baion among the Hebrews is the tender branch.' The Greek grammarians derive it from 'to be plucked by force.' Balsamon says it is a Latin word, others say Egyptian. But who does not know the follies of the etymologists? The so-called Alexandrian Chronicle, p. 7821: 'And the wife came to the emperor Valentinian with the palm early in the morning.' Read either 'with the palm' or 'of the palms.' And a woman came with a palm in the morning to the emperor Valentinian; or: and a woman came to the emperor Valentinian on the morning of Palm Sunday.

unplaced.en: 'Boukinou', 'boukinon' and 'bykinon': a trumpet (buccina). Hence 'boukinator' and 'bykinator' (trumpeter). In the Jus Graeco-Romanum, p. 49, 'bikinator', but 'bykinator' is preferable, as on pp. 232 and 506; also in Blastares, p. 72 E.

unplaced.text: Καταρώμεθα. In Zachariam Cyrillus, p. 673 D. Τοῦτό τι παθεῖν ἐπειρᾶτό τινα τῶν εἰς Χριστὸν δεδυσσεβηκότων ὁ μακάριος Δαβίδ, λέγων· Καὶ διάβολος στήτω ἐκ δεξιῶν αὐτοῦ. Sed non dubito quin scripserit ἐπηρᾶτο. Ad hunc sensum: Hoc ut contingeret cuidam in Christum impiorum, imprecabatur beatus David dicens: « Diabolus stet a dextris ejus. » Psal. cviii, 6, de Juda. Parque mendum offendes in Anastasii quæst. 62, p. 410: Τί δὲ οἱ θαυμάσιοι Πέτρος καὶ Παῦλος; οὐχὶ ὁ μὲν θάνατον ἐπὶ Ἀνανίαν καὶ Σαπφείραν ἐπήγαγεν; ὁ δὲ πήρωσιν Ἐλύμᾳ τῷ μάγῳ ἐπαγόμενος (imo ἐπαρώμενος vel cum cod. Reg. 1789, ἐπαρασάμενος) ἐπήνεγκε: Quid vero admirabiles illi Petrus et Paulus? Annon ille mortem attulit Ananiæ et Saphiræ? Hic autem, Elymam magum exsecratus orbavit oculis?
unplaced.anchorLine: μεθα (h). Ὡς ὅταν λέγομεν· « Ἐλέησόν με, ὁ Θεός,
unplaced.en: 'We curse.' Cyril on Zechariah, p. 673 D: [Greek: the blessed David tried to bring this upon one of those who had been impious toward Christ, saying: 'Let the devil stand at his right hand']. But I do not doubt that he wrote 'ἐπηρᾶτο.' To this sense: that this might befall one of the impious against Christ, blessed David was calling down a curse, saying 'Let the devil stand at his right hand' (Ps. 108:6), about Judas. You will find the same fault in Anastasius, question 62, p. 410: [Greek: And what of the wondrous Peter and Paul? Did not the one bring death on Ananias and Sapphira, and the other, inflicting blindness on Elymas the magician (rather 'invoking a curse', or with Royal codex 1789 'having cursed'), bring it about?] That is: What of those admirable men Peter and Paul? Did not Peter bring death on Ananias and Sapphira? And did not Paul, cursing Elymas the magician, deprive him of sight?

unplaced.text: Αἰσχύνην. Ἰσχὺν volebat scribere.
unplaced.anchorLine: ἐκλείπειν τὴν αἰσχύνην (i) μου μὴ ἐγκαταλίπῃς με.
unplaced.en: 'Shame.' He meant to write 'strength' (ἰσχύν).

unplaced.text: Ἐπίτασις. Corrupte apud Cyrillum, ad Joan. xiii, 6, t. IV, p. 722 D, impressum est στάσιν pro τάσιν. Τὸ ἀπονίζεσθαι τοὺς πόδας, μετρίως ἀποχαλᾷ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ βαδίσματος τάσιν· Pedum ablutio aliquantum relaxat et resolvit distensionem ex incessu ortam. Item in Epistolis Nili, lib. III, epist. 142, ἀνάστασιν pro ἀνάτασιν· Καὶ πάντως ἐπάνω φανείημεν τῆς δυσθυμίας, τῆς δολουργῶς ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκαθάρτων πνευμάτων ἡμῖν ὑποσπειρομένης, πρὸς τὸ παραλῦσαι ἡμῶν καὶ ἐκνευρίσαι τὴν δικαίαν ἀνάτασιν· Et omnino supra tristitiam esse appareamus, quæ in nobis insidiose ab impuris spiritibus disseminatur, ad dissolvendam et enervandam justam nostram contentionem. Editio Possini epist. 99, Ἔννοιαν.
unplaced.anchorLine: ἀδελφοί· ἀλλ' ἡ τῆς ἀσκήσεως ἐπίτασις (j) ἀποσβεν-
unplaced.en: 'Intensity.' Corruptly in Cyril, on John 13:6, vol. 4, p. 722 D, 'στάσιν' is printed for 'τάσιν'. [Greek: Washing the feet moderately relaxes the strain from walking.] That is: the washing of the feet relaxes somewhat and loosens the strain arising from walking. Likewise in the Letters of Nilus, bk. 3, letter 142, 'ἀνάστασιν' for 'ἀνάτασιν': [Greek quoted]: and let us by all means appear above the despondency craftily sown in us by unclean spirits to loosen and unnerve our rightful striving. The edition of Possinus, letter 99, has 'Ἔννοιαν'.

unplaced.text: Hoc epithetum vir omni laude major Carolus Fresnius, in Dissertatione de inferioris ævi numismatibus, cap. 67, ponit in nummo Heraclii: longe rectius quam ii qui legendum putaverant, λογοθέτης, νομοθέτης. Quanquam ἀθλοθέτης propius accedit ad ectypum; ut cuilibet patebit.
unplaced.anchorLine: δόξα, καὶ ταύτην ὁ ἀγωνοθέτης (k) τοῖς ἀγωνιζομέ-
unplaced.en: This epithet Charles Du Fresne (Du Cange), a man above all praise, in his Dissertation on the coinage of the later age, ch. 67, places on a coin of Heraclius: far more correctly than those who thought one should read 'logothetes' or 'nomothetes'. Although 'athlothetes' comes closer to the impression, as will be plain to anyone.

unplaced.text: Ἠνέσχετο. Hom. 25, Paschali sancti Cyrilli, p. 299 C: Οἱ γὰρ ἀκάθεκτοι πρὸς πλεονεξίαν, ἀεὶ τοῖς οὖσι προστιθέναι σπουδάζοντες τὰ οὐκ αὐτοῖς μᾶλλον, τοῖς δὲ πέλας προσήκοντα, τάχα που καὶ μόνοι τὴν γῆν οἰκήσιμον ἔχειν ἐπείγονται, γειτόνων οὐκ ἀνεχόμενοι. Non ἀπεχόμενοι: Qui enim immoderata cupiditate habendi laborant, semper iis quæ possident adjicere studentes ea quæ ad vicinos potius, quam ad ipsos spectant, quodammodo soli habitare terram conantur, qui finitimos pati non possint.
unplaced.anchorLine: ἠνέσχετό (l) ποτε, ἵνα ἄλλος αὐτῷ γεμίσει ὕδωρ·
unplaced.en: 'He endured.' Paschal Homily 25 of St Cyril, p. 299 C: [Greek: for those unrestrained in greed, always eager to add to what they have what is not theirs, and rather what belongs to their neighbours, perhaps even strive to hold the habitable land alone, not tolerating neighbours]. [The editor notes 'Not ἀπεχόμενοι' (not 'refraining').] Latin: For those who labour under immoderate desire of having, always eager to add to what they possess what pertains to their neighbours rather than to themselves, in a way try to inhabit the earth alone, since they cannot bear neighbours.

unplaced.text: Ἐσχόλαζεν εἰς τὰ καλιγραφία. Infra Balsamon, De jejuniis, n. 21: Ποῖος κανὼν ταύτας ἐκαλιγράφησε; Καλλιγραφίας δυσδιόρθωτον τέχνην appellat auctor Vitæ Nili junioris, p. 57. Et in Anastasii Hodego, p. 204, ubi habetur: Πρὸς Γεώργιον τὸν πρεσβύτερον, καὶ λογογράφον τῆς ἐκκλησίας αὐτῶν, τὸν λεγόμενον Κλειδοποιόν. Exemplar Regium 1052 καλλιγράφον exhibet atque καχθιδοποιόν; Juris Græco-Romani p. 1, p. 470, καλλιγραφήσαντας ἢ καχιγραφήσαντας; actione 14 sextæ synodi, καλῶς καλλιγραφεῖ.
unplaced.anchorLine: ὀλίγα βιβλία· ἐσχόλαζεν δὲ εἰς τὰ καλιγραφία (m).
unplaced.en: 'He was occupied with calligraphy.' See below, Balsamon, On Fasts, n. 21: 'What canon wrote these out in a fair hand?'; the author of the Life of Nilus the Younger, p. 57, calls it 'the art of calligraphy, hard to correct'. And in Anastasius's Hodegos, p. 204, where we find: 'To George the presbyter and scribe of their church, called the Locksmith (Kleidopoios).' The Royal copy 1052 offers 'kalligraphon' and 'kathidopoion'; Jus Graeco-Romanum, part 1, p. 470, 'those who had written fair' or 'kachigraphesantas'; in action 14 of the sixth synod, 'he writes well'.

unplaced.text: Αὐτὸς ἤψει. Doctrina II Dorothei, ante medium: Μὴ, τὸ ἔψῃ τὸ καλῶς. Leg. Μὴ τὸ ἔψητο καλῶς. Non illud recte coctum fuerat. Scribi etiam posset, ἐψητὸν, res cocta.
unplaced.anchorLine: πηρεσίας ἀνεχόμενος· αὐτὸς ἤψει (n), αὐτὸς ἔπλυ-
unplaced.en: Autos hepsei [He himself boiled]. Dorotheus, Doctrine 2, before the middle: 'Μὴ, τὸ ἔψῃ τὸ καλῶς.' Read: 'Μὴ τὸ ἔψητο καλῶς' (lest what was boiled not be done well). What he had cooked had not been right. One could also write ἐψητόν, 'a cooked thing'.

unplaced.text: Nactus sum ista in codice Regio 1026, f. 188: Ὅρος τῆς ἁγίας καὶ οἰκουμενικῆς τετάρτης συνόδου Πατέρων ἁγίων ἐν Χαλκηδόνι, οἷς ἦν ἀριθμὸς ἑπτὰ συνθέτους ἔχων δραμούσας εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἐννάδας. Hoc est: Definitio sanctæ et œcumenicæ quartæ synodi Patrum sanctorum apud Chalcedonem, quorum numerus septem compositos continebat in se recurrentes novenarios. Ex hac ergo opinione fuerunt Patres Chalcedonenses numero duntaxat 567.
unplaced.anchorLine: τῶν σ', καὶ ἡ ἐν Καλχηδόνι ⁶⁸ χλ' (ο). Καὶ ὅταν ἔλθῃ ὁ
unplaced.en: I found this in the Royal codex 1026, fol. 188: 'Definition of the holy and ecumenical fourth synod of the holy Fathers at Chalcedon, whose number, containing seven composite (numbers), ran into itself nines.' That is: the definition of the holy and ecumenical fourth synod of the holy Fathers at Chalcedon, whose number contained within itself seven compound recurring novenaries. From this opinion, therefore, the Fathers of Chalcedon were only 567 in number.

unplaced.text: Βρεκτά. Ordo monasterii Casulorum laudatus per Allatium, De missa præsanctificatorum, n. 7: Ἐσθίομεν ἄρτον, καὶ φάβα βρεκτόν. Comedimus panem, et fabam aqua maceratam. Moschi nostri, cap. 163, Ἄρτον καὶ βρεκτά· interpres, panem et cicer infusum; e mss. Καὶ ἐρεβίνθια βρεκτά.
unplaced.anchorLine: κτὰ (p), ἔρχεται εἰς τὴν ἔρημον· καὶ τῷ νέῳ διὰ τῆς
unplaced.en: Brekta [soaked things]. The rule of the monastery of the Casuli, cited by Allatius, De missa praesanctificatorum, n. 7: 'We eat bread and soaked beans' (Latin: we eat bread and beans macerated in water). In our Moschus, chap. 163: 'Bread and brekta'; the translator renders it bread and soaked chickpea; from the manuscripts: 'and soaked chickpeas, brekta'.

unplaced.text: Σημειογράφου. Invenies in Lexicis, ut et σημειογραφεῖν. At σημειογραφεῖον non invenies, quod legitur pag. paulo ante citata Hodegi Anastasiani, statim post verba relata: Συγκαθεζομένων ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ σημειογραφείῳ τοῦ Καισαρίου. Apud Allatium, De perpetua consensione, etc., col. 674: Ἀπὸ τῶν σιγνογραφίων. Theodorus Studita, De sancto Platone, n. 16: Ἐσυρμαιογράφησεν. Ἐσπουδαιογράφησεν; Aristeas, χρυσογραφία; Syncellus, βίβλοι κεχρυσογραφημέναι.
unplaced.anchorLine: σημειογράφου (s) τελείως, καὶ παρὰ τοῦ γραμματι-
unplaced.en: Semeiographou [of the notary]. You will find this in the Lexicons, as also semeiographein. But semeiographeion you will not find, though it is read on the page cited a little earlier from the Hodegos of Anastasius, right after the words quoted: 'While we were sitting together in the notary's office of Caesarius.' In Allatius, On the Perpetual Agreement, etc., col. 674: 'From the signographia.' Theodore the Studite, On Saint Plato, n. 16: 'He wrote ...' 'He wrote with zeal'; Aristeas, 'gold-writing'; Syncellus, 'books written in gold.'
unplaced.unreadable: Printed under the heading NOTAE (a Greek-column endnote block at foot, after VARIAE LECTIONES). Mark is printed '(s)' with the second letter small; read as s (consistent with lettered series). Some Greek forms in the Theodorus Studita citation are damaged ('Ἐσυρμαιογράφησεν').

unplaced.text: Ἐλεύθερον. Ἐλεύθερος, liber, ingenuus, honestus, probus, ἐλευθέρα, libera, ingenua, honesta, matrona, uxor. Sic apud Cyrillum Alexandrinum, lib. VII Contra Julianum, p. 229 A: Ἐλευθέρα γυνιχί. Et τὴν εὔφυᾶ καὶ ἐλεύθερον, p. autem 244 D. Γάμων ἐλευθέρων λησταί. Occurritque ἐλευθέρας nomen sæpe in Basilio, Chrysostomo, Palladio, Moscho, aliisque; interdum vero imperitia librariorum evasit in ἐλευθερίαν, ut apud Chrysostomum non semel observarunt viri docti. Cui adde Basilium, epist. 188, cum Nostro cap. 188. Sed et puto Palladium in Dialogo de vita Chrysostomi, p. 155, scripsisse: Οὐ τῷ σκοπῷ τῆς ἐλευθέρας προσέχων, ἀλλὰ τοῖς Θεοφίλου θρύλλοις. Scopo probæ mulieris non attendens, sed Theophili fabulis. Loquitur de Olympiade, quamquam ἐλευθερίας retineri posset, atque exponi de libertate et liberalitate.
unplaced.anchorLine: τητος εἰσελθόντος πρὸς τὸν ἐλεύθερον (t) κατὰ τὸ
unplaced.en: ἐλεύθερον. Ἐλεύθερος means free, freeborn, honorable, upright; ἐλευθέρα, free woman, freeborn, honorable, matron, wife. So in Cyril of Alexandria, book 7 Against Julian, p. 229 A: 'a free woman'; and 'the well-born and free', and on p. 244 D 'robbers of free marriages'. The noun ἐλευθέρας occurs often in Basil, Chrysostom, Palladius, Moschus and others; sometimes through the ignorance of copyists it has slipped into ἐλευθερίαν, as learned men have noted more than once in Chrysostom. Add Basil, epistle 188, with our own chapter 188. And I think Palladius wrote in the Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom, p. 155: 'not heeding the aim of the free (noble) woman, but the tales of Theophilus', meaning heeding not the respectable woman's purpose but Theophilus's fables. He is speaking of Olympias, although ἐλευθερίας could be kept and be explained of freedom and generosity.

unplaced.text: Ζιχία. Non memini me alibi legere. Interpres Ambrosius, capsulas. Quod potest esse βιβλία.
unplaced.anchorLine: τοῖς· Φέρετε τά μου ζιχία (u). Καὶ ἤνεγκαν. Καὶ
unplaced.en: Ζιχία. I do not remember reading it elsewhere. The translator Ambrosius has 'capsulas' (little boxes). It may be βιβλία (books).

unplaced.text: Περιοδευθῆναι. Ad quid explicarem verbum quod obscurum non est? Cur ergo Nota? Ut emendetur sancti Nili epistola 285, lib. II: Ἵνα γνῷς σαφέστατα καὶ τοῦ ἐχθροῦ τὴν μανίαν, καὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ τὴν κηδεμονίαν, θᾶττον περιοδεύσαντός σε, ὡς εὐνούστατον δοῦλον. Ut clarissime cognoscas et adversarii rabiem, et Christi sollicitudinem, qui te veluti servum dilectissimum quantocius curavit. Περιοδυνήσαντος; contrarium plane sensum reddit.
unplaced.anchorLine: θεν εἰς πόλιν τινὰ περιοδευθῆναι (v) Ὑπεδέξατο
unplaced.en: Περιοδευθῆναι. Why should I explain a word that is not obscure? Why then a Note? So that the epistle of St Nilus, no. 285, book 2, may be emended: 'Ἵνα γνῷς ... δοῦλον', that is, 'that you may know most clearly both the adversary's rage and Christ's solicitude, who cared for you as a most beloved servant, and as quickly as possible'. Περιοδυνήσαντος (having caused pain) gives a plainly contrary sense.

unplaced.text: Σιανθείς. Verbum minus usitatum Dorothei, doctrina 71: Εἶδον πολλοὺς τῶν ἀδελφῶν ὑβρίζοντας καὶ σιαίνοντας αὐτόν. Aspiciebam multos fratres contumelia afficientes et commoventes seu irritantes ipsum.
unplaced.anchorLine: ταῦτα παρ' αὐτῆς καὶ ἄλλα τοιαῦτα, σιανθεῖς (x)
unplaced.en: Σιανθείς. A rather unusual word of Dorotheus, teaching 71: 'I saw many of the brothers insulting and vexing him.' (Latin: I saw many brothers treating him with insult and stirring or provoking him.)

unplaced.text: Καμάτους. In Auctario novissimo Combefisii, t. I, p. 199 B. Irenæus, Ὁ ὄνος τύπον εἶχε σώματος Χριστοῦ· ἐφ' ὃν πάντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἐκ καμάτων ἀναπαυόμενοι, ὡς ὑπ' ὀχήματος βαστάζονται. Vix quemquam dubitaturum arbitror, quin legi debeat καμάτων. Asina Balaami, figura erat corporis Christi; super quem cuncti homines a laboribus quiescentes, velut curru gestantur.
unplaced.anchorLine: ἡδονὴν ἀπολέσαι τοὺς τοιούτους καμάτους (y) ὅσους
unplaced.en: Καμάτους (labors). In Combefis's latest Auctarium, vol. 1, p. 199 B. Irenaeus: 'The ass was a type of the body of Christ, on which all people, resting from their labors, are carried as in a vehicle.' I think hardly anyone will doubt that one should read καμάτων. Balaam's ass was a figure of Christ's body, on which all men, resting from their labors, are carried as in a carriage.

unplaced.text: Πλεονεκτεῖ. Accipitur πλεονεκτεῖν in bonam et in malam partem: in bonam, apud Cyrillum, in Nahum, p. 477 E: Ὤοντο γὰρ ὅτι νενικήκασι οὐκ ἑκόντος αὐτοῦ, καὶ ὁμοῦ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐπαμύνουσαν αὐτοῖς πεπλεονεκτήκασι χεῖρα. In malam, apud eumdem, ad Michæam, p. 452 D: Ἐπονηρεύσαντο, πεπλεονεκτήκασιν (sic malo quam πεπλεονάκασιν) καὶ διωγμοὺς εἰργάσαντο κατὰ τῶν ἁγίων.
unplaced.anchorLine: Εἶπεν πάλιν ὁ γέρων· Πλεονεκτεῖ (z) ὁ ταπεινὸς
unplaced.en: Πλεονεκτεῖ. The verb πλεονεκτεῖν is taken both in a good and in a bad sense. In a good sense, in Cyril on Nahum, p. 477 E: 'for they thought they had conquered not with his consent, and together with the Jews they have gained the advantage over the hand that defended them.' In a bad sense, in the same on Micah, p. 452 D: 'They acted wickedly, they have overreached (so I prefer this to πεπλεονάκασιν) and carried out persecutions against the saints.'

unplaced.text: Ἱκανήν. Tollo per levem occasionem leve mendum ab Aristea De LXX, quæst. 17: Μὴ πολλῶν ὀρέγου, τῶν δ' ἱκανῶν πρὸς τὸ βασιλεύειν. Interpr. Neque multas jurisdictiones ad tuum regnum pertrahere cupias; scribendo τῶν δὲ ἱκανῶν. Hoc est: Ne multa cupias, sed quæ sufficiunt ad regnandum.
unplaced.anchorLine: νὴν (a) ὥραν, ἕως οὗ συστείλαι καὶ ἐκ τοῦ μέσου τὰ
unplaced.en: Ἱκανήν. I remove, on a slight pretext, a slight error, taken from Aristeas, On the LXX, question 17: 'Do not strive after many things, but those sufficient for reigning.' The translator: 'Do not desire to draw many jurisdictions into your kingdom', by writing τῶν δὲ ἱκανῶν. That is: do not desire many things, but what suffices for ruling.

unplaced.text: Καθαρά. Ex sensu verti bellaria. Neque enim alibi ejusmodi significatione inveni. At interpres Ambrosius quod non intelligebat, laxius transtulit. In Glossariis, καθαρὸς ἄρτος, Siliginenm. Quid vero sit cœna pura neminem latere potest.
unplaced.anchorLine: μοι ὀλίγα ὠά, καὶ ὀλίγα καθαρά (b). Λέγω αὐτῷ·
unplaced.en: Καθαρά. I translated it by sense as 'bellaria' (sweetmeats). For I have not found the word in such a meaning elsewhere. The translator Ambrosius, because he did not understand it, rendered it loosely. In the Glossaries, καθαρὸς ἄρτος is 'Siliginenm' (wheaten bread). What a pure supper is, no one can fail to know.

unplaced.text: Φώτισμα. Quemadmodum Ecclesia vocatur locus in quo fit cœtus, ἐκκλησία, ita hoc capite et sequenti φώτισμα dicitur locus in quo illuminatio, φώτισμα, baptismus, celebratur: qui locus vulgo nominatur φωτιστήριον, φωτιστήρ, βαπτιστήριον, βαπτιστήρ, baptisterium. An vero apud alium scriptorem φώτισμα hoc sensu accipiatur, plane nescio. Non tamen multum dissimiliter in Symmictis Allatii, p. I, p. 36 et 62, locus est βάπτισις, et βάπτισις Χριστοῦ. Quod vero spectat ad φώτισμα seu φωτισμὸν, baptismum, observavi Theodorum Gazam interpretem Orationum sancti Chrysostomi de incomprehensibili Dei natura, orat. 4, p. 775 A, t. I, posuisse post sacri lavacri splendorem, pro eo quod Græce est, μετὰ τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν τοῦ λουτροῦ. Quia nimirum legebat, ἀπόφαυσιν, nomine minus usitato. Quemadmodum διαφαύματος scripserat auctor Martyrii SS. Maximi, Dudæ et Quintiliani, n. 3. (Qua voce etiam utitur Cyrillus Scythopolita in Vita Sabæ, cap. 17 et 67.) Ediderunt autem, διαφαίματος, et tentaverunt corrigere, διαυγάσματος. Ad Aprilis 13, Pseudochrysostomus, De turture, seu De Ecclesia: Εἴ τις ἐστιν ἐνταῦθα κατηχούμενος, μετανοείτω, προσερχέσθω τῷ Θεῷ, τῷ ὕδατι βαπτιζέσθω, τῷ βλέμματι (an πνεύματι) φωτιζέσθω.
unplaced.anchorLine: λεως Κοιανέων, ἐν ᾗ ἐστιν φώτισμα (c), ἐν τοῖς
unplaced.en: Φώτισμα. As the place where an assembly takes place is called Ecclesia (ἐκκλησία), so in this chapter and the next φώτισμα is the name of the place where illumination (φώτισμα), that is baptism, is celebrated; the place commonly called φωτιστήριον, φωτιστήρ, βαπτιστήριον, βαπτιστήρ, baptisterium. Whether φώτισμα is taken in this sense in another writer, I do not know at all. Yet something not very different is found in Allatius's Symmicta, part 1, pp. 36 and 62: the place is 'baptism', and 'baptism of Christ'. As to φώτισμα or φωτισμός, baptism, I have noted that Theodorus Gaza, translator of the Orations of St Chrysostom On the Incomprehensible Nature of God, oration 4, p. 775 A, vol. 1, put 'after the splendor of the sacred bath' for the Greek 'after the enjoyment of the bath', since he evidently read ἀπόφαυσιν, a less common noun. As the author of the Martyrdom of SS Maximus, Dada and Quintilian, no. 3, had written διαφαύματος (the same word is also used by Cyril of Scythopolis in the Life of Sabas, chs. 17 and 67). They have printed διαφαίματος and tried to correct to διαυγάσματος. On 13 April, Pseudo-Chrysostom, On the Turtle-dove, or On the Church: 'If anyone here is a catechumen, let him repent, come to God, be baptized with water, be illumined by the sight (or perhaps by the Spirit).'

unplaced.text: Σπόριμα. Ex Glossis, sationes, sata, segetes, a σπείρω. Quod verbum misere prima littera truncatum jacet in Auctario Combefisiano primo, c. 841 E, ubi Gregorius Antiochenus de sepulcro Dominico loquentem sic introducit angelum: Δεῦτε, ἴδετε τὸν τόπον ἐν ᾧ παρεὶς ὁ ἄσπορος κόκκος τῷ
unplaced.anchorLine: πορευώμεθα, ηὑρέθημεν εἰς τὰ σπόριμα (d), καὶ κατ-
unplaced.en: Σπόριμα. From the Glossaries: 'sationes, sata, segetes' (sowings, sown fields, crops), from σπείρω. This word lies sadly truncated at its first letter in Combefis's first Auctarium, col. 841 E, where Gregory of Antioch, speaking of the Lord's tomb, introduces the angel saying: 'Come, see the place in which ... the unsown grain ...' (the note breaks off at the foot of the page, mid-sentence, at 'τῷ'; presumably continues on p-0169).
unplaced.unreadable: note is cut off at the page foot after 'τῷ' (continuation, if any, on next page)

unplaced.text: σώματος, πολύχνουν ἄσταχυν ἀθανασίας ἐβλάστησε. Venite, videte locum, in quo granum non satum solutum corpore, numerosam immortalitatis spicam germanavit. Sed quis dubitaverit quin scribendum sit σπαρείς, ad hunc sensum, in quo satum granum illud corporis quod sine semine prodiit?
unplaced.anchorLine: (on p-0168) πορευώμεθα, ηὑρέθημεν εἰς τὰ σπόριμα (d), καὶ κατ-
unplaced.en: ...body, it put forth the many-seeded ear of immortality. (Latin:) Come, see the place in which a grain not sown, loosened in the body, has sprouted a numerous ear of immortality. But who could doubt that one must write σπαρείς (sown), to this sense: in which the sown grain, that of the body which came forth without seed?
unplaced.unreadable: continuation of note (d) begun at foot of p-0168; one Greek word in the first line (read πολύχνουν) is partly blurred

unplaced.text: Nudam eam sancto oleo inungere.] Obtinuit olim tam viros quam feminas nudas corporibus baptizare, itaque inungere.
unplaced.en: In the past it was customary to baptize both men and women naked in body, and therefore to anoint them.

unplaced.text: Saracenos.] De monachis a Saracenis interfectis Martyrologium Romanum 19 Februarii: « In Palæstina commemoratio sanctorum monachorum, et aliorum martyrum, qui a Sarracenis sub duce Alamundaro ob fidem Christi sævissime cæsi sunt. » Ubi Baronius notat: Iisdem cæsi sunt hi Sarracenorum incursionibus, quarum mentio habetur in rebus gestis sancti Joannis Silentiarii, quas refert Metaphrastes die 13 Maii, itemque in Vita sancti Sabæ abbatis apud eumdem die 5 Decembris, ac in Actis et in sancti Euthymii abbatis, quæ idem recitat die 20 Januarii. Consentiunt iisdem quæ habentur in Prato spirituali, cap. 21 et ?9. Una eademque persecutio Sarracenorum sanctos monachos diversisque diebus occidit, ut non mireris si inferius de monachis cæsis a Sarracenis sæpe agatur. Hactenus Baronius.
unplaced.en: On the monks killed by the Saracens, the Roman Martyrology for 19 February: 'In Palestine, commemoration of the holy monks and other martyrs who were most cruelly slain by the Saracens under their leader Alamundarus for the faith of Christ.' Baronius notes there: these were killed in the same Saracen raids mentioned in the acts of St John the Silentiary (which Metaphrastes gives on 13 May), likewise in the Life of St Sabas the abbot (same author, 5 December), and in the Acts of St Euthymius the abbot (same author, 20 January). What is found in the Spiritual Meadow, chapters 21 and ?9, agrees with these. One and the same Saracen persecution killed holy monks on different days, so you need not wonder that later there is frequent talk of monks killed by Saracens. So far Baronius.
unplaced.unreadable: chapter number after 'cap. 21 et' is damaged ('?9')

unplaced.text: Ex scholaribus.] In Græco est, ἀπὸ Σχολαρίων. Hervetus verterat scholasticus. Ex militiæ ordine scholares sunt.
unplaced.en: In the Greek it is 'from the Scholarii'. Hervetus had translated 'scholasticus'. The 'scholares' belong to the order of the army.

unplaced.text: Verba sanctæ oblationis.] Infra, cap. 196, habes item verba oblationis a puero prolata, et panem una cum saxo, quod pro altari erat, igne cœlesti consumptum; quod reverentiæ causa factum credo, ne videlicet tam sanctum mysterium puerilibus ludicris exponeretur.
unplaced.en: Below, ch. 196, you have likewise the words of the oblation spoken by a boy, and the bread together with the stone that served as an altar consumed by heavenly fire; I believe this was done out of reverence, lest so holy a mystery be exposed to children's games.

unplaced.text: Babylæ.] Ut hic ecclesiam ingrediens, audita fortuita Evangelii sententia ad meliorem frugem convertitur, idem pluribus aliis contigit. Vide dicta ad Vitam sancti Antonii cap. 2, n. 9.
unplaced.en: As here someone entering a church, hearing a chance saying of the Gospel, is turned to a better life, the same happened to many others. See what is said on the Life of St Anthony, ch. 2, no. 9.

unplaced.text: Eliæ.] De Elia in exsilium misso exstat mentio in Vita sancti Sabæ, auctore Cyrillo, 5 Decemb. Vide Baronium, tomo VI, anno Christi 513, Symmachi papæ 15, Anastasii imp. 23, et Theodorici regis 21. Quod vero hic habetur, post duos dies, monet Baronius tomo eodem, anno Christi 518, Hormisdæ papæ 5, Anastasii imp. 28, Theodorici regis 26, duos, inquiens, nimirum dies a scriptis litteris, non autem ab obitu Anastasii numerandos. Certe in Vita sancti Sabæ a Cyrillo monacho conscripta, 5 Decembris, Elias ipse ex visione et revelatione narrat se decimo die Anastasium ea hora mortuum secuturum.
unplaced.en: Of Elias sent into exile there is mention in the Life of St Sabas by Cyril, 5 December. See Baronius, vol. 6, year of Christ 513, Symmachus pope 15, Anastasius emperor 23, Theodoric king 21. As for what is read here, 'after two days', Baronius warns, same volume, year 518, that the two days are to be counted from the writing of the letters and not from Anastasius's death. Certainly in the Life of St Sabas written by Cyril, 5 December, Elias himself says from a vision and revelation that he would follow Anastasius in death on the tenth day, at that hour.

unplaced.text: Accendamus ignem.] Frequens ea in causa fidei ad ignem provocatio. Exempla aliquot congessi in dissertat. de Fide hæreticis servanda cap. 12.
unplaced.en: Appeal to fire was frequent in matters of faith. I have collected some examples in my dissertation on keeping faith with heretics, ch. 12.

unplaced.text: Anastasii.] Baronius, tomo VI, anno Christi 495, Gelasii papæ 4, Anastasii imp. 5, Theodorici regis 3, agit de Euphemio in exsilium misso ab Anastasio; anno vero Christi 511, Symmachi papæ 13, Anastasii imp. 21, Theodorici regis 19, de Macedonio in exsilium ab eodem Anastasio pulso. Quæ hic habes de quatuordecim deletis, intellige de annis. Zonaras, tomo III, in Anastasio: Καὶ αὖθις ὄναρ ἰδεῖν λέγεται ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐκεῖνος, ἄνδρα τινὰ φοβερὸν, τόμον κατέχοντα, καὶ λέγοντα πρὸς αὐτόν· Ἰδοὺ διὰ τὴν κακοπιστίαν σου, ἀπαλείφω τῆς ζωῆς σου ἔτη τεσσαρεσκαίδεκα: « Denuo aliud vidisse somnium memoratur rex, virum terribilem, qui librum manu gestaret et diceret: Ecce ob perversitatem fidei tuæ, annos XIV vitæ duæ deleo. » Vide Baronium, tomo VI, anno Christi 518, Hormisdæ papæ 5, Anastasii imperatoris 28, Theodorici regis 26.
unplaced.en: Baronius, vol. 6, year of Christ 495, treats of Euphemius sent into exile by Anastasius; and in 511, of Macedonius driven into exile by the same Anastasius. What you have here about the 'fourteen deleted', understand as years. Zonaras, vol. 3, under Anastasius: 'And again that emperor is said to have seen in a dream a fearsome man holding a scroll and saying to him: Behold, because of your bad faith I blot out fourteen years of your life.' (Latin: Again the king is said to have seen another dream, a terrible man holding a book in his hand and saying: Behold, because of the perversity of your faith I delete fourteen years of your life.) See Baronius, vol. 6, year 518, Hormisdas pope 5, Anastasius emperor 28, Theodoric king 26.

unplaced.text: Minutorum viginti.] Existimo in Græco fuisse λεπτῶν vel φόλεων, nam deest hic nobis ille textus. Infra, cap. 134: « Accipiebatque quotidianum stipendium novem minuta. »
unplaced.en: I think the Greek had λεπτῶν or φόλεων, for that text is missing here. Below, ch. 134: 'And he received a daily wage of nine minuta.'

unplaced.text: Et de adoratione.] Septima synodus generalis, quæ est secunda Nicæna, actione 4 et 5 exemplum hoc ex hoc libro Græce citat.
unplaced.en: The seventh general synod, which is the second Nicene, in its 4th and 5th sessions cites this example from this book in Greek.

unplaced.text: Lictores qui assistebant.] Græce φραγγελιβαί. Intelligit lictores ducis. Hervetus verterat, et cæteri qui assistebant.
unplaced.en: In Greek 'φραγγελιβαί'. It means the duke's lictors (attendants). Hervetus had translated 'and the others who were standing by'.

unplaced.text: Ut canonarchæ.] Hoc Herveto deerat. Appositum ex Græco, in quo κανόναρχος, id est, qui canoni psalmorum cantandorum præest.
unplaced.en: Hervetus lacked this. It is added from the Greek, which has κανόναρχος, that is, one who presides over the canon of psalms to be sung.

unplaced.text: Senum gesta.] In Græco est βιβλίον Γεροντικόν. Ita liber ille appellabatur. Ex Gerontico ms. quædam vertit Raderus noster parte III Viridarii sui. Sic Verba Seniorum dicebantur quæ Patres illi scite proferebant.
unplaced.en: The Greek has 'Gerontikon book'; that book was so called. Our Raderus translated some things from a manuscript Gerontikon in part 3 of his Viridarium. 'Sayings of the Elders' was likewise the name of what those Fathers wisely uttered.

unplaced.text: Mittite thymiama in thuribulum.] Jam olim in honorem sanctorum thymiama incendi solitum.
unplaced.en: Already of old incense was customarily burned in honor of the saints.

unplaced.text: Thalelæi.] Raderus noster, Viridarii parte I, putat hunc eumdem cum Thalelæo martyre tempore Numeriani, de quo Menæa, 20 Maii. Sed vereor ut ratio temporis aliud suadeat: siquidem Moschus audivit ex Petro, quæ de hoc hic habentur; at Petrus centenis annis a Numeriani imperio distat. Aliter
unplaced.en: Our Raderus, in part 1 of the Viridarium, thinks this man the same as the martyr Thalelaeus in the time of Numerian, of whom the Menaea, 20 May. But I fear the chronology suggests otherwise: Moschus heard from Peter what is told here about him, and Peter is a hundred years distant from Numerian's rule. Otherwise ... (the note breaks off at the foot of the page with 'Aliter').
unplaced.unreadable: note breaks off after 'Aliter' at the foot of the page; continues on p-0171

unplaced.text: (continuation) opinandi occasio forte fuit, quod hic dicatur Cilix; et alter in Menæis dicatur Azarbi in Cilicia abditus. Sed ibidem dicitur profectus a Libano; quare Libanites est. Verisimilius hunc eumdem esse cum Thalelæo Theodoreti, cap. 28 Philothei, quia uterque Cilix, et idem de pœnitentia dictum habent. Theodoretus eum vidit, et Moschus audivit narrari ex Petro. Sic tempora convenire potuerunt.
unplaced.en: (Continued from p-0170) ...the occasion for the opinion was perhaps that this man is called a Cilician, and the other in the Menaea is said to be (Azarbi) hidden in Cilicia. But there he is said to have set out from Lebanon, so he is a Lebanese. It is more likely that he is the same as Theodoret's Thalelaeus (Philotheus, ch. 28), since both are Cilicians and have the same thing said about repentance. Theodoret saw him, and Moschus heard it told by Peter. In this way the dates could agree.
unplaced.unreadable: one letter of 'Azarbi' ambiguous (b/h); this block is the continuation at the top of the page, preceded by 'Aliter' at the foot of p-0170

unplaced.text: Per Serapim facite.] Ita locus hic nunc restitutus ex Græco. Ante nullo sensu erat, Serapim facite.
unplaced.en: This place is now restored from the Greek in this way. Before, it made no sense: 'Serapim facite'.

unplaced.text: Carabum.] Ex sequentibus intelligitur quid carabus sit. Dicitur enim: Produc scapham.
unplaced.en: From what follows one understands what a 'carabus' is. For it is said: 'Bring out the boat.'

unplaced.text: Tetrapylum.] Porticus vel templum quatuor columnarum ordinibus constans. In Græco omittitur, ad Orientem juxta Tetrapylum; ejus loco est, τὴν ἐπονομαζομένην τῆς Δωροθέας: quæ cognominabatur Dorotheæ, de beatæ Virginis æde. Tetrapyli Alexandrini meminit Sophronius archiepiscopus Hierosolymitanus, agens de miraculis Joannis et Cyri martyrum: Εἴσελθε γοῦν εἰς Ἀλεξάνδρειαν, καὶ ἐν τῷ μεγάλῳ Τετραπύλῳ νήστης καθεύδησον: « Ingredere itaque Alexandriam, et in magno Tetrapylo jejunus dormi. » Quæ citantur in septima synodo, act. 4.
unplaced.en: Tetrapylum: a portico or temple consisting of four rows of columns. In the Greek 'to the east beside the Tetrapylum' is omitted; in its place is 'the one called of Dorothea', i.e. which was surnamed Dorothea's, of the church of the Blessed Virgin. Sophronius, archbishop of Jerusalem, mentions the Alexandrian Tetrapylum in his account of the miracles of John and Cyrus the martyrs: 'Go into Alexandria, and in the great Tetrapylum sleep fasting.' These words are cited in the seventh synod, session 4.

unplaced.text: Epitimia.] Retinui Græcam vocem ἐπιτίμια, id est, multas. Ecclesiastici quidam scriptores Latini hoc usurpant vocabulum. Vide Onomasticon.
unplaced.en: I kept the Greek word epitimia, that is, penalties. Some Latin ecclesiastical writers use this word. See the Onomasticon.

unplaced.text: Quibus manibus.] Manibus olim viri, feminæ linteolo Eucharistiam excipiebant et sumebant.
unplaced.en: In the past men received and took the Eucharist in their hands; women with a linen cloth.

unplaced.text: Apocrisiarii.] Infra, cap. 145, misso quodam apocrisiario suo. Est fere apocrisiarius, Græcis ἀποκρισιάριος, legatus ecclesiæ negotia tractans.
unplaced.en: Below, ch. 145: 'having sent a certain apocrisiarius of his'. An apocrisiarius, in Greek ἀποκρισιάριος, is roughly an envoy handling the affairs of a church.

unplaced.text: Templum sancti Quirici.] Videndum an non hic ipse, qui sanctus Quiriacus in Romano Martyrologio dicitur, 29 Septembris: « In Palæstina sancti Quiriaci anachoretæ, » cujus Vitam a Metaphraste descriptam apud Laurentium Surium eo mense habes.
unplaced.en: It should be considered whether this is not the same man who is called St Quiriacus in the Roman Martyrology, 29 September: 'In Palestine, of St Quiriacus the anchorite', whose Life written by Metaphrastes you have in Laurentius Surius under that month.

unplaced.text: Sarraceni.] Vide hic dicta supra, ad cap. 21, de Sarracenorum incursionibus, et martyribus sub iis passis.
unplaced.en: See what is said above, at ch. 21, about the Saracen raids and the martyrs who suffered under them.

unplaced.text: Responsum.] Quid hic responsum sit, jure hæreas. Suspicor in Græco fuisse προσφωνάριον, quod interpres prima et obvia notione responsum vertit. Videndum tamen num hic vertendum sit, sportam, vel simile quid. Suggerebat videlicet monacho cogitatio, ut non adoraret crucem, sed in cellam rediret, et sportas texeret. Vide dicta sup., ad lib. v, libel. x, n. 18. Quod si responsum hic communi notione intelligitur, cape fratrem hunc missum pro responsis cœnobii. Sic infra, cap. 235: « aliquis manens in cœnobio missus est pro responsis cœnobii. »
unplaced.en: You may rightly hesitate over what 'responsum' is here. I suspect the Greek had a word (garbled in the print, something like προσφωνάριον), which the translator rendered 'responsum' by its first and obvious meaning. It should be considered whether it ought rather to be translated 'sporta' (basket) or something similar: the thought suggested to the monk that he not worship the cross but return to his cell and weave baskets. See what is said above on book 5, booklet 10, no. 18. But if 'responsum' is taken in its ordinary sense, understand this brother as sent for the replies of the monastery. So below, ch. 235: 'someone living in a monastery was sent for the monastery's replies.'
unplaced.unreadable: Greek word printed with damaged letters (read προσφωνάριον by shape, uncertain); chapter number 235 has a damaged middle digit

unplaced.text: Cantheliam.] Sunt canthelia, κανθήλια, onera asinis imponi solita.
unplaced.en: 'Canthelia' (κανθήλια) are loads usually placed on asses.

unplaced.text: Sibino.] Idem mox accurrit caput 123: « vestitum colobio de sibino. » Quid sibinum sit, nondum mihi lectum.
unplaced.en: The same word soon occurs in chapter 123: 'clothed in a colobium of sibinum'. What sibinum is, I have not yet read.

unplaced.text: Burdones.] Vide dicta ad Vitam Simeonis Stylitæ, cap. 20, n. 24.
unplaced.en: See what is said on the Life of Simeon Stylites, ch. 20, no. 24.

unplaced.text: In sancta Christi Dei nostri resurrectione.] Hoc loco Resurrectio est templum Christi resurrectioni dicatum.
unplaced.en: In this place 'Resurrection' is the temple dedicated to Christ's resurrection.

unplaced.text: Syncello seu assessori suo.] Servavi Græcum vocabulum syncellus, qui apud Græcos est proximus a patriarcha.
unplaced.en: I kept the Greek word 'syncellus', who among the Greeks is next to the patriarch.

unplaced.text: In membranis valde pulchrum.] Græce est: ἐν σώματι πολὺ καλῷ.
unplaced.en: The Greek is: 'in a very fair body'.

unplaced.text: Zachariæ.] Zachariam non perfecte credidisse angelo, Lucas, cap. 1, testatur. Non dubitavit Zacharias de Dei potentia, qui noverat Isaacum de sterili Sara et Abrahamo genitum, sed de voluntate Dei. Quare in supplicium dubitationis cessit illi taciturnitas. Augustinus lib. L Homiliarum, homil. 44: « Accepit Zacharias supplicium taciturnitatis, merito infidelitatis: quia non credidit, tacuit; sic enim recte dictum est psalmo cxv: Credidi, propter quod locutus sum; quia Zacharias non credebat, merito non loquebatur. » Ambrosius, lib. II in Lucam: « Incredulitas Zachariæ affatum eripuerat et auditum. »
unplaced.en: Luke, ch. 1, testifies that Zacharias did not fully believe the angel. Zacharias did not doubt God's power, he who knew that Isaac was born of barren Sarah and Abraham, but doubted God's will. Hence silence became the punishment of his doubt. Augustine, book 50 of the Homilies, homily 44: 'Zacharias received the punishment of silence, deservedly for unbelief: because he did not believe, he was silent; for it is rightly said in Psalm 115: I believed, therefore have I spoken; because Zacharias did not believe, he deservedly did not speak.' Ambrose, book 2 on Luke: 'The unbelief of Zacharias had taken away his speech and hearing.'

unplaced.text: Leone.] Baronius, tomo VI, anno Christi 449, Leonis papæ 10, Theodosii 42, Valentiniani 25, impp., ad hanc de Leonis encyclica (quæ inter epistolas Leonis est 10) visionem notat: Sed præstat, inquit, audire potius sententiam Petri, quam visionem Petri, dicentis: Firmiorem quavis visione habemus sermonem propheticum (II Pet. I), etc. Etenim majorem sibi ea epistola fidem vindicat ex divinis Scripturis, traditionibusque sanctæ Ecclesiæ, et communi sanctorum Patrum consensu, quam ex recensita modo visione. Hactenus Baronius. Qui ad sequentis capitis visionem de sancto Eulogio defensore epistolæ sancti Leonis ista quoque addit: At certioris fidei certiorisque quoque testimonii apud me est de epistola sancti Leonis publica concilii œcumenici Chalcedonensis assertio et prædicatio, quam quælibet privatæ hujusmodi visiones. Ita Baronius. Vide apud eumdem plura de hac Leonis encyclica elogia. Ad sequens caput 149, de Leone ita notat Baronius anno 461, Hilarii papæ 1, Leonis 5, et Severi 1, impp. Sed quid est: Omnia tibi sunt dimissa peccata, præter manuum impositionem? Num peccata ex parte dimitti possunt? Minime gentium, si ad culpam referas. Cæterum quoad pœnam dici debent dimissa fuisse sancto Leoni peccata. Quod enim facile sit in his peccare etiam prudentem episcopum, jure sanctus Apostolus monet ita Timotheum: Nemini cito manus imposueris, neque communicaveris peccatis alienis (I Tim. V). Illis ergo remanebat sanctus Leo delictorum pœnis obligatus, quæ illi perpetrassent, qui ab eo indigne promoti fuissent ad ordines. Tunc namque dicuntur præsules communicare peccatis alienis, dum indignis conferunt honores et ministeria. Hinc sibi timens Propheta rex, ait: Ab alienis parce servo tuo (Psal. XVIII). Quod si hæc fiunt in viridi, quid fiet in arido (Luc. XXIII)? Leone quis sanctior atque prudentior, ut tantum periculum liber transiliat?
unplaced.en: Baronius, vol. 6, year of Christ 449, Leo pope 10, emperors Theodosius 42 and Valentinian 25, notes on this vision about Leo's encyclical (which is letter 10 among Leo's letters): 'But it is better, he says, to hear Peter's judgment rather than Peter's vision, when he says: We have a more sure prophetic word than any vision (2 Pet. 1), etc. For that letter claims greater credit for itself from the divine Scriptures, from the traditions of holy Church and the common consent of the holy Fathers than from the vision just recounted.' So far Baronius. He adds on the vision in the following chapter concerning St Eulogius, defender of St Leo's letter: 'But of surer faith and surer testimony in my view is the public assertion and proclamation of the ecumenical council of Chalcedon about St Leo's letter than any private visions of this kind.' So Baronius; see more in him on this encyclical eulogy of Leo. On the next chapter, 149, Baronius notes about Leo in the year 461, Hilary pope 1, Leo 5, Severus 1, emperors: 'But what is this: All your sins are forgiven, except the laying on of hands? Can sins be forgiven in part? By no means, if you refer it to guilt. But as regards punishment, the sins can be said to have been remitted to St Leo. For that even a prudent bishop may easily sin in these matters, the holy Apostle rightly warns Timothy: Lay hands hastily on no man, neither be partaker of other men's sins (1 Tim. 5). So St Leo remained liable to the penalties of the offenses committed by those whom he had unworthily promoted to orders. For then prelates are said to share in others' sins when they confer honors and ministries on the unworthy. Hence the prophet-king, fearing for himself, says: Spare thy servant from the sins of others (Ps. 18). But if these things happen in the green wood, what will happen in the dry (Luke 23)? Who is holier and wiser than Leo, to leap clear of so great a danger?'

unplaced.text: Flabellum.] Græco ῥιπίδιον. Ejus in sacro faciendo usus, quod diaconus gestat.
unplaced.en: In Greek ῥιπίδιον. It is used in performing the sacred rite, and the deacon carries it.

unplaced.text: Conopionem.] Servavit interpres Græcam inflexionem, quod nunc κωνωπεῖον, nunc κωνωπεών dicitur, conopeum Latinis usitatum, pro textili tentorio culicibus arcendis comparato.
unplaced.en: The translator kept the Greek inflection, which is called now κωνωπεῖον, now κωνωπεών; Latin writers use 'conopeum', for a woven tent made to keep off gnats.

unplaced.text: Membranas.] Ut hic membranas ad aquam pluviam excipiendam explicant, sic alii nautæ vellera et pelles exponunt, tum ad pluviam tum ad rorem colligendum.
unplaced.en: As here they spread out skins to catch rainwater, so other sailors put out fleeces and hides, either to collect rain or dew.

unplaced.text: Arena.] Nec arena littoralis, nec quocunque modo madefacta potest esse materia baptismi; siquidem materia baptismi aqua esse debet, qua quis ablui possit. Vide Scholasticos in III partem divi Thomæ, et in primis Franciscum nostrum Suarez, t. III, in III partem, ad q. 66, art. 4, disp. 20, sect. 1.
unplaced.en: Neither beach sand nor sand wetted in any way can be the matter of baptism; since the matter of baptism must be water, by which one can be washed. See the Scholastics on the third part of St Thomas, and especially our Francisco Suárez, vol. 3, on the third part, q. 66, art. 4, disp. 20, sect. 1.

unplaced.text: Infusa.] Quæ hæc infusa sint, difficile divinare. Nam varii cibi infundi possunt et macerari. Hic ante: « paucisque infusis cibariis. » Aliquoties in Theodoreto supra habens « lentem aqua madefactam. » Hic infra, cap. 184: « Infundebat et paximatia seu madefaciebat. »
unplaced.en: What these 'infusa' are is hard to guess, for various foods can be soaked and softened. Earlier here: 'and a few soaked foods'. Several times above in Theodoret, 'lentils soaked in water'. Here below, ch. 184: 'He soaked or moistened the biscuits.'

unplaced.text: Chrysostomus.] Henricus Savilius, notis suis ad tomum VIII Chrysostomi Græce a se editi, existimat non indignum observatu temporibus inter quintam synodum, anno 553, et sextam, anno 680 celebratam (quibus Georgium Vitæ Chrysostomi scriptorem vixisse probabile esse ait) Chrysostomi cognomen ignotum fuisse. Sed refellit eum Joannes Moschus seu Sophronius hic, qui tempore Georgii istius vixere, et hujus cognominis Chrysostomi meminere.
unplaced.en: Henry Savile, in his notes on vol. 8 of Chrysostom (edited by him in Greek), thinks it worth observing that in the period between the fifth synod (553) and the sixth (680), in which he says George, the writer of Chrysostom's Life, probably lived, the surname Chrysostom was unknown. But John Moschus or Sophronius here refutes him: they lived in that George's time and mention this surname of Chrysostom.

unplaced.text: Gregorii.] Habetur hæc narratio in Vita sancti Gregorii, lib. II, cap. 45 per Joannem Diaconum scripta, qui eam citat ex libro, qui a Græcis Λειμών dicitur, a Latinis vero intelligitur Campus vel Pratum. Qui hic ipse liber est, quem præ manibus habemus. Citat ille ex interpretatione præceptoris sui, ubi quod hic est, tunicam non habeo, vertit ille, casulam non habeo. Eodem modo idem, lib. IV, c. 63: « Et jussit mihi dari casulam, et necessitates meas omnes. » Ubi noster interpres Ambr. Camaldulensis hic, cap. 181: « Jubens mihi dari quæcunque erant necessaria, » decurtate. Omisit enim illud de casula seu tunica.
unplaced.en: This story is in the Life of St Gregory, book 2, ch. 45, written by John the Deacon, who cites it from the book called Leimon by the Greeks, which the Latins understand as Campus or Pratum (Meadow). This is the very book we have in hand. He cites it from the translation of his teacher, where our text's 'I have no tunic' he renders 'I have no chasuble'. In the same way, book 4, ch. 63: 'And he ordered a chasuble given to me, and all my needs.' Where our translator Ambrose of Camaldoli here, ch. 181, has 'ordering all necessities to be given to me', abridged; for he omitted the part about the chasuble or tunic.

unplaced.text: Nomicum seu dispensatorem.] Varia Nomici, Νομικοῦ, ut hic in Græco textu, est significatio. Hic dispensatorem significat.
unplaced.en: 'Nomicus' (Νομικοῦ), as here in the Greek text, has various meanings. Here it means a steward or dispenser.

unplaced.text: A notario perfecte, et a grammatico sufficienter.] Notarius hic est qui præest pueris ad prima elementa et litteras formandas. Vide Onomasticon.
unplaced.en: Here the 'notarius' is the one who presides over boys for the first elements and for forming letters. See the Onomasticon.

unplaced.text: Idcirco sunt baptizati.] Baronius, tomo III, anno Christi 310, § 13. Significat nimirum ejusmodi sacramentum consecutos, non autem, quod aiunt, rem sacramenti, ipsam gratiam abluentem peccata.
unplaced.en: Baronius, vol. 3, year of Christ 310, section 13. It means that they obtained the sacrament as such, but not, as they say, the thing of the sacrament, the very grace washing away sins.
